title: 深度优先搜索与回溯法

text: Go deep, undo, try the next choice: queens, mazes, partitions, flood fill.

lines: A1 A2 go deep first (green),back up at a dead end, try the next

text: Depth-first search (DFS) explores one choice all the way down before trying the next. When a branch fails or is finished, it backtracks: undoes the last choice and tries another. Written as recursion, the call stack remembers where to come back to.
Template: check the goal; for each possible move: if allowed, mark it, recurse, unmark it. Forgetting to unmark is the most common backtracking bug.

One queen per row, so the recursion goes row by row. Each column and each diagonal holds at most one queen: cells on the same "/" diagonal have the same r + c, cells on the same "\" diagonal have the same r − c (shifted by n so the index is not negative). Three boolean arrays make every check O(1) (P1219).
To count all paths that never revisit a cell, mark a cell when you step on it and unmark it when you step back, so later paths may use it again (P1605).
This explores every path, which grows exponentially: fine for a 5 × 5 maze, hopeless for 50 × 50. For the shortest path use BFS (14.2) instead.

Keeping each part at least as large as the one before (minPart ) lists every split exactly once and already in order (P2404). The same "choose → recurse → undo" lists subsets (选数 P1036, PERKET P2036, 第10章).

Pruning cuts branches that cannot win: stop when the partial cost already exceeds the best answer found (吃奶酪 P1433), or when the remaining choices cannot reach the goal. Order choices so good answers are found early, which makes the cut stronger.

Scan the grid; each time you meet unvisited water, that is a new lake, and a DFS "sinks" every connected cell so it is not counted again (P1596). No unmarking here: a cell belongs to exactly one region.
Searching a fixed word in 8 directions (P1101) and chaining words by overlaps (P1019) are DFS with a different "move" step.
Layer by layer with a queue: shortest steps on boards and between states.

Breadth-first search (BFS) explores in layers: first every cell 1 step away, then every cell 2 steps away, and so on. The first time a cell is reached is therefore by a shortest path, when every move costs 1.
Use a queue (first in, first out): take the front cell, push its unvisited neighbours with distance + 1. Mark a cell as visited when you push it, so it is never queued twice.

DFS (14.1) BFS (14.2) order one branch to the end, then back up layer by layer DFS (14.1) BFS (14.2) tool recursion (stack) queue good for all solutions, counting, regions, backtracking fewest steps when each step costs 1 memory the current path the current layer

dist[][] = -1 doubles as the "visited" mark. queue<pair<int, int>> stores a cell as two numbers; q.front().first and .second read them. Each cell enters the queue once, so the whole BFS is O(n × m) (P1443). left << setw(5) prints each number left-aligned in 5 columns.
BFS works on any states joined by moves of cost 1, not just grid cells. Here a state is a floor and the two buttons are the moves (P1135).

The same idea finds the fewest rule applications turning one string into another, with map<string, int> as the distance table (P1032); time steps (P2895) and teleporters (P1825) only change which moves exist.

Cells inside a closed loop are exactly the 0s that cannot be reached from outside. So flood the outside instead: start from the border and mark every reachable 0; whatever 0 is left unmarked is inside (P1162).
A padding ring of 0s around the grid joins all border cells into one region, so one BFS start at (0, 0) covers the whole outside.
The Luogu problems for this chapter, a ladder through them, and experiments to try yourself.
Key points to memorise
1. DFS: go deep, then backtrack; template: check goal → for each move: mark, recurse, unmark.
2. Forgetting to unmark is the classic backtracking bug.
3. Queens: one per row; columns c, diagonals r + c and r − c + n in boolean arrays.
4. Counting all paths is exponential; for the shortest path use BFS.
5. List each combination once: keep choices non-decreasing.
6. Prune: stop when the partial cost already reaches the best answer.
7. Flood fill: each unvisited cell starts a new region; no unmarking.
8. BFS = layers with a queue; first visit = shortest when every move costs 1.
9. Mark visited when pushing; dist = −1 can serve as "not visited".
10. States can be floors, strings or positions with time; only the moves change.
11. Inside a loop = cells not reachable from outside: flood from the border.
